title: Choosing a practice
hookLine: fit, a good teacher, community, and an ethical frame

lines: THE ONE YOU FORGET YOU'RE WEARING.
cards: A shoe store, a Saturday afternoon. The runner on the bench has tried on six pairs. One pair is beautiful and pinches.
One is what a well-known athlete wears and slides off the heel. Finally the salesperson says something useful: walk to the back of the store and back, and tell me which one you forget you're wearing.
After weeks visiting the world's schools of practice, a fair question is waiting. Which of these, if any, would you actually wear every day? Not the most impressive.
Not the one a friend swears by. The one that fits.

teach.b: Four questions, each worth slowing down for. First, fit. Does this practice suit your body, your temperament, your days?

Someone with a bad knee may not sit cross-legged for an hour. Someone who thinks best while moving might find walking or slow movement easier than stillness. Someone who loves words may be drawn to reading and reflection.
Fit isn't laziness: a practice you can keep beats a grand one you abandon. Second, a good teacher.
Not a well-known one: someone who has done the practice a long time, is honest about its limits, and welcomes your questions. Third, community.
Practice is easier in company, and company keeps you honest. A group that sits, sings or studies together will notice when you stop showing up.
Fourth, an ethical frame. Several schools on this tour came with one: precepts, commandments, virtues, vows. A technique without a way of living around it can drift.
Two old texts give a way to test all four.

In the Buddhist Kalama Sutta, in paraphrase, the Buddha tells a group of confused villagers not to go by rumor, tradition or a teacher's reputation alone, but to notice for themselves which things lead to harm and which to well-being, and choose accordingly.
And in the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus gives a short test for telling true prophets from false: "Ye shall know them by their fruits."
Each text speaks in its own setting, and each asks you to watch what a practice actually grows in a person, over time.

how: People choosing a practice often try several, look for a teacher with long experience who welcomes questions, join a group that practices together, and keep the practice inside an ethical frame such as precepts, commandments or vows; in some traditions a newcomer simply starts by attending and asking.

o: trying every practice once and keeping none for long
weighing fit, teacher, company and ethics before you commit
picking whichever practice is most well-known right now

s: the best practice is the most demanding one
a practice you can actually keep beats a grand one you abandon. fit isn't laziness.
in the Kalama Sutta, the Buddha says to judge by what leads to harm or well-being
he tells the villagers not to go by rumor, tradition or reputation alone, but to notice for themselves.
a good teacher is a well-known one
the lesson's test is long practice, honesty about limits, and welcoming your questions.

games.q: the villagers in the Kalama Sutta are confused: every visiting teacher praises his own way and runs down the others. what does the Buddha tell them?
o: follow the teacher with the best reputation.
notice for yourselves what leads to harm and what to well-being.
stay with the tradition you were born into, no questions.
games.why: he tells them not to go by rumor, tradition or a teacher's reputation alone, but to watch what things actually lead to, and choose accordingly.

practice: Take the four questions one by one, slowly. What fits your body and your days right now, not in some ideal year?

What would you want from a teacher, do you need company or quiet, and what way of living would you want a practice to sit inside? Let one honest word come for each; it doesn't have to be a good answer.

wordCard.voice: Choosing a practice. Four questions: fit, a good teacher, community, and an ethical frame, tested by what the practice grows in a person. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: what fits. A practice you can keep beats a grand one you abandon. See you on the path.
